I recognized that this finding was a fruit of a plant, as the fruit of the eastern black walnut is round, with a thick and green husk, as the one shown in the picture is. The plant is the Eastern Black Walnut tree, and the fruit is characterized by a husk with a hard nut inside, and it is covered in irregular furrows. It has edible, sweet, oily meat that matures in late summer to fall. Tress may produce seed crop after only 4 years of growth. However, large seed crops do not occur until the trees are between 20 and 30 years old. Even then, good seed crops are produced irregularly, averaging 2 good seed crops every 5 years. 
(The Eastern Black Walnut is a tree of the Genus and Species Juglans nigra. The average height of this tree is 15.80 meters.The Eastern black walnut grows best in coves and well-drained bottoms, as found in the Appalachians and the Midwest. It does well particularly well along streams and on the lower portion of slopes facing northeast. It is commonly found on limestone soils. It does not do well on wet bottom land and on sandy, dry ridges and slopes. )

description:
Native
1014

"Black walnut is an important tree commercially, as the wood is a deep brown color and easily worked. The fruits, walnuts, are cultivated for their distinctive and desirable taste. Often, trees are grown for both lumber and walnuts simultaneously and many cultivars have been developed for improved quality nuts or wood. Black walnut is currently under pressure from the thousand cankers disease that is causing decline of walnuts in some areas. Black walnut is also allelopathic, which means that it releases chemicals from roots and other tissues that harm some other organisms and give the tree a competitive advantage.

Strong taproot makes them difficult to transplant.

The nuts are food for many rodents and make up to 10% of the diet of eastern fox squirrels.[7] The nuts are also eaten by species of birds. The leaves are browsed by white tailed deer,[7] although they are not a preferred food. Squirrels benefit this species by distributing and burying the seeds; if the seeds are not reclaimed by the squirrel, they will germinate and help disperse the species.

Black walnut drupes contain juglone (5-hydroxy-1,4-naphthoquinone), plumbagin (yellow quinone pigments), and tannin. These compounds cause walnuts to stain cars, sidewalks, porches, and patios, in addition to the hands of anyone attempting to shell them.[15] The brownish-black dye was used by early American settlers to dye hair.[16][better source needed] 

Industrial

Walnut shells are often used as an abrasive in sand blasting or other circumstances where a medium hardness grit is required. The hard black walnut shell is also used commercially in abrasive cleaning, a filtering agent in scrubbers in smoke stacks, cleaning jet engines, cosmetics, and oil well drilling and water filtration.

Wood


Black walnut is highly prized for its dark-colored, straight grained, true heartwood. It is heavy, strong, shock resistant and yet can be easily split and worked. Along with cedars (Thuja spp.), chestnut (Castanea spp.), and black locust (Robinia pseudoacacia) black walnut is one of the most durable hardwoods in the US.[7] The wood can be kiln dried and holds its shape well after seasoning, which makes this wood even more attractive for wood working.[7]

Walnut wood has historically been used for gun stocks, furniture, flooring, paddles, coffins, and a variety of other wood products.[7] Due to its value, forestry officials often are called on to track down walnut poachers; in 2004, DNA testing was used to solve one such poaching case, involving a 55-foot (16-m) tree worth US$2,500. I am fixing my original observation of this tree that I made when I first joined iNaturalist, when I had all the pictures in the same observation. They are now separated by the date they were taken, with the earliest in October 2017 and the last in February 2021.

I no longer live here, but you can ask anyone in either attached building if you can come into the yard to collect seeds in the fall, they probably won't care at all. 

This tree has produced fruit since at least before 2017.

Some pictures show the tree with a chain wrapped around it. The chain was put on it before I lived there, and it wasn't until right before I moved out that I finally figured out how to remove it. The chain has been removed, so you don't need to worry about that causing damage to the tree, though unfortunately I wasn't able to remove the metal stake that was put through to hold the chain in place.

It also looked like something had been eating on the fruit (photos 4 & 5).

description:
As you can tell by the number of photos, I was excited to see several butternut trees, from large to seedling-sized, when I toured a friend's farm property. We have a blight in this area that kills butternuts, so they aren't common here and this is only the second time I've seen one locally.
I think these were wild, though they could have been planted. The previous homeowner liked butternuts, and the smaller tree we saw was in a flowerbed near the house, but the placement made me think this might be a "let stand" tree, where the homeowner recognized a squirrel planted seedling and just didn't cut it. There was a mature butternut at the edge of the woods dropping nuts, and I saw several probably squirrel-planted seedlings around the property.
There were also plenty of black walnuts on the property, so I was able to make some comparisons. Butternuts have much larger leaves and much broader leaflets than walnuts, and I got several shots of big butternut leaves. Overall, butternuts are much hairier and stickier than walnuts, as they are densely covered in glandular hairs. You can see this from my leaf closeup and from the golden-velvety fuzz on the butternut fruit. My hands felt sticky after handling those leaves and fruits. Butternut fruits are fuzzy and oval, whereas walnut fruits are hairless and round. I lined up a couple of young walnuts next to some butternuts to show that difference. Finally, butternut bark, both on young and mature trees, is relatively smooth, as opposed to the deeply ridged bark you'd see on a black walnut.

5 trees ranging from 5-6 to 12-13 inch diameter.  Fruits present on the larger trees.  Brown chambered pith.  5 seedlings across trail to east.  1 more pole size to west.  All within a 1 city block stretch along Iron Belle Trail which was railroad grade.  North side except the 5 seedlings.  Scattered (fewer) black walnut seedlings and saplings also present.  1 block away, 1 mature butternut next to house, seemingly younger based on size, than biggest tree along trail.  Seedlings also occur along the side of a couple other houses going east on Lowell St., probably "planted" by squirrels.  Walnut seedlings alongside houses in neighborhood also.   Additional trees found in vicinity on subsequent visits.

Walnuts and butternuts scattered in thicket area along Iron Belle Trail which was a railroad grade.  1 pole-size and 1 sapling walnut.  White chambered pith.  No terminal leaflet. Smells strongly of walnut.  No fruits seen. Also 1 sapling and 1 seedling to west of biggest butternut.  All within one city block stretch of trail on north side. Some walnut seedlings near houses in the neighborhood and used to be a mature walnut tree that produced a lot of fruits, now cut down.

description:
Eastern Black Walnut (Juglans nigra)

19 August 2024
9000 4th Street & 6900 Oak Street
Frisco, Denton County, Texas

Nota: Came upon one of Frisco’s older residential areas and an empty lot whose house had long been cleared with its large, old trees still standing and including a huge Eastern Cottonwood, a huge Pecan tree with bountiful large pecans on its stems, two of the largest/tallest (and endangered) American Elms I’ve seen in Denton County, a large Sugar Hackberry, and so on—old trees. Squirrels and other critters like birds had left evidence of the fact they harvest what these trees have to offer. A very small stream runs alongside the entire length of one of the lot’s sides allowing snails, water plants, crayfish, and other life forms to thrive in wetter times. There were crayfish holes (homes) dug into the soil across the entire lot, perhaps as many as 100 or more. This indicates the lot has been houseless for a long time. Developers are clearly targeting the space for redevelopment, as evidenced by another such lot across the street that had an overly large sign announcing its being for sale. Same old story, narrative. I was impressed that our quick walk (and unplanned survey) rendered some interesting observations. Glad we had a chance to see this older (earlier settled/developed) side of the city. The new Frisco is one subdivision after another, one strip mall after another, one new and coming store after another, etc. It’s grow, grow, grow. The City of Frisco is in both Denton and Collin counties. I believe this area we stopped to observe for signs of life is actually in Collin County.
